options.a: How much a material spreads light into colors
options.b: How much a material slows/bends light
options.c: How much UV light a material absorbs
options.d: How hard a material's surface is to scratch

distractorExplanations.a: Spreading light into colors is dispersion, which the Abbe value describes; index describes how much light slows and bends.
distractorExplanations.c: UV absorption depends on the material's UV cutoff and any absorber, not on its index of refraction.
distractorExplanations.d: Scratch resistance is a hardness/hard-coat property; index of refraction concerns the speed of light in the material.

options.a: Speeds up and bends away from the normal
options.b: Keeps its speed but changes wavelength
options.c: Slows and may refract
options.d: Changes color as its frequency drops

distractorExplanations.a: Glass has a higher index than air, so light slows and bends toward the normal; it does not speed up and bend away.
distractorExplanations.b: Speed and wavelength drop together in glass (v = f x wavelength); frequency is what stays constant at the boundary.
distractorExplanations.d: Frequency, and so perceived color, stays the same when light enters a new medium; speed and wavelength change instead.

options.b: Brightness (intensity) of the light
options.c: Lens power in diopters
options.d: Degree of polarization of light

distractorExplanations.b: Brightness relates to the amplitude/intensity of the light wave, not its wavelength, which sets the perceived hue.
distractorExplanations.c: Lens power depends on surface curves and index; wavelength is a property of the light itself, not of the lens.
distractorExplanations.d: Polarization describes the plane in which the light wave vibrates, which is independent of its wavelength.

options.b: Lens diameter increases
options.c: Power in diopters increases
options.d: Abbe value increases

distractorExplanations.a: Focal length is the reciprocal of power (f = 1/D), so lower power gives a longer focal length, not a shorter one.
distractorExplanations.b: Lens diameter affects field of view and edge thickness; it does not change the focal length of the lens.
distractorExplanations.d: Abbe value describes dispersion (chromatic aberration); it does not determine focal length or lens power.

options.b: The cylinder axis
options.c: The 90° meridian
options.d: The base

distractorExplanations.a: The optical center is the point of zero prism; prismatic displacement is described by base and apex, not the OC.
distractorExplanations.b: The cylinder axis is the meridian of no cylinder power; it does not set the direction of prismatic image shift.
distractorExplanations.c: The 90-degree meridian is a vertical reference line; prism direction is named by base (up, down, in, out), not a meridian.

options.a: Convergence/divergence of a pencil of rays
options.b: The bending of light at a single surface
options.c: The splitting of white light into colors
options.d: The reflection of rays off the front lens surface

distractorExplanations.b: Bending at a surface is refraction; vergence is the degree to which a pencil of rays converges or diverges.
distractorExplanations.c: Splitting white light into colors is dispersion, described by the Abbe value, not vergence.
distractorExplanations.d: Reflection off a lens surface is what AR coating manages; vergence describes rays spreading apart or converging.

options.a: Seen only by looking back through the lens
options.b: Formed by a plane mirror
options.c: Projected/focused onto a screen
options.d: Formed by a minus lens from a real object

distractorExplanations.a: Images seen by looking back through the optics are virtual; real images form where rays actually converge.
distractorExplanations.b: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image behind the mirror, which cannot be caught on a screen.
distractorExplanations.d: A minus lens diverges light from a real object, so it forms a virtual image, not a real one.

options.b: Dispersion by wavelength
options.c: Light loss from surface reflections
options.d: Image size change from lens power

distractorExplanations.a: Oblique astigmatism is a monochromatic aberration from viewing off-axis, not a wavelength-dependent effect.
distractorExplanations.c: Reflection losses are handled by AR coating; chromatic aberration comes from wavelengths bending by different amounts.
distractorExplanations.d: Image size change is spectacle magnification, driven by power and vertex distance, not by dispersion of wavelengths.

options.b: The refractive index of a lens material
options.c: The UV cutoff wavelength of a material
options.d: The impact resistance of a lens material

distractorExplanations.b: Refractive index describes how much a material bends light; the Abbe value describes how much it disperses colors.
distractorExplanations.c: UV cutoff is a separate material property; the Abbe value measures dispersion, with lower numbers meaning more fringing.
distractorExplanations.d: Impact resistance is tested with drop-ball standards; the Abbe value relates to chromatic dispersion, not toughness.

options.b: Real inverted images
options.c: Virtual inverted images
options.d: Real upright images

distractorExplanations.b: Real inverted images come from concave mirrors with the object beyond F; a plane mirror forms virtual images.
distractorExplanations.c: Plane-mirror images are upright, though laterally reversed; they are not inverted top to bottom.
distractorExplanations.d: A plane-mirror image lies behind the mirror and cannot be projected, so it is virtual, not real.

options.b: Forms a real upright image
options.c: Can form a real inverted image
options.d: Forms a real, inverted, enlarged image

distractorExplanations.a: A virtual upright image forms when the object is inside F of a plus lens, not when it is beyond 2F.
distractorExplanations.b: Real images from a single plus lens are inverted; an upright image from a plus lens is a virtual one.
distractorExplanations.d: An object beyond 2F gives a diminished real image; an enlarged real image needs the object between F and 2F.

options.b: Thicker at edges than center
options.c: Equal in thickness at center and edge
options.d: Thicker at the top edge than the bottom

distractorExplanations.c: Equal center and edge thickness describes a plano lens with no power, not a minus lens.
distractorExplanations.d: A thicker top edge describes base-up prism, not the center-to-edge thickness profile of a minus lens.
distractorExplanations.a: Not the best answer: Thicker at center than edges.

options.b: Thicker at the nasal edge than temporal
options.c: Equal in thickness across the lens
options.d: Thicker at center than edges

distractorExplanations.a: A thin center with thick edges describes a minus lens; plus lenses are thickest at the center.
distractorExplanations.b: A thicker nasal edge describes base-in prism, not the center-to-edge thickness profile of a plus lens.
distractorExplanations.c: Uniform thickness describes a plano lens with no power; plus power requires a thicker center.

options.b: Plastic lens material
options.c: High-index glass lens material
options.d: Thermoplastic frame material

distractorExplanations.a: CR-39 is a thermoset allyl resin; polycarbonate is a different thermoplastic with higher impact resistance and index.
distractorExplanations.c: CR-39 is a plastic with an index of about 1.498; it is neither a glass nor a high-index material.
distractorExplanations.d: CR-39 is a lens material; frame thermoplastics include materials such as nylon and TR-90, not CR-39.

options.a: High Abbe value and minimal color fringing
options.b: Scratch resistance without needing a hard coat
options.c: Impact resistance and thinner profile vs some plastics
options.d: Lighter weight and a higher Abbe value than CR-39 lenses

distractorExplanations.a: Polycarbonate has a low Abbe value (about 30), so it shows more chromatic aberration, not less.
distractorExplanations.b: Polycarbonate is a soft material that scratches easily, so it is supplied with a factory hard coat.
distractorExplanations.d: Polycarbonate is lighter than CR-39, but its Abbe value (about 30) is far lower than CR-39's (about 58).

options.a: Raise the Abbe value for clearer peripheral vision
options.b: Reduce thickness/weight for stronger powers
options.c: Reduce reflections without needing AR coating
options.d: Lower the lens power needed for the same Rx

distractorExplanations.a: Higher-index materials usually have lower Abbe values, so they increase color fringing rather than reduce it.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher index increases surface reflections, so high-index lenses need AR coating more, not less.
distractorExplanations.d: The prescribed power stays the same; high index reaches that power with flatter, thinner surfaces.

options.b: Surface reflections
options.c: Surface scratches
options.d: Light transmission

distractorExplanations.a: AR coatings cut reflected light; UV transmission is blocked by the lens material or a UV absorber.
distractorExplanations.c: Scratch resistance comes from a hard coat; AR layers reduce reflections and can even make scratches more visible.
distractorExplanations.d: AR coating increases light transmission by cutting reflections; it does not reduce the light passing through.

options.b: Darken more in hot weather
options.c: Darken in response to bright indoor light
options.d: Darken with UV exposure

distractorExplanations.a: Most windshields block UV, so standard photochromic lenses darken very little inside a car.
distractorExplanations.b: Photochromics darken less in heat, because warmth speeds the reaction that fades them back to clear.
distractorExplanations.c: Indoor light contains little UV, so standard photochromic lenses stay mostly clear indoors.

options.b: Glare from horizontal reflections
options.c: Glare from vertically polarized light
options.d: Image blur from high astigmatism

distractorExplanations.a: Blue-light filtering is a separate coating or absorber; polarizing film blocks horizontally polarized glare.
distractorExplanations.c: Polarized lenses have a vertical transmission axis, so vertically polarized light passes; horizontal glare is blocked.
distractorExplanations.d: Polarization does not correct optical blur; astigmatism needs cylinder power in the prescription.

options.a: Improve cosmetics and optics for certain powers
options.b: Add base-in prism to ease convergence at near
options.c: Correct astigmatism without cylinder power
options.d: Raise the Abbe value of the lens material

distractorExplanations.b: Prism is ordered in the Rx; aspheric surfaces flatten the lens and reduce peripheral aberrations instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Astigmatism still needs cylinder power; aspheric curves reduce off-axis aberrations, not ocular astigmatism.
distractorExplanations.d: Abbe value is a fixed property of the material; aspheric surfaces change lens shape, not material dispersion.

options.a: A lined segment with intermediate power
options.b: A corridor of increasing minus power
options.c: A single power across the whole lens
options.d: A corridor of increasing plus power

distractorExplanations.a: A visible line with an intermediate zone describes a trifocal; progressive lenses blend power with no lines.
distractorExplanations.b: Power in a progressive corridor increases in plus toward the near zone, not in minus.
distractorExplanations.c: One power across the lens describes a single-vision lens; a progressive changes power along the corridor.

options.a: Manage horizontal prism imbalance at distance
options.b: Manage vertical imbalance in anisometropia
options.c: Thin the edges of high minus lenses
options.d: Reduce image size difference in aniseikonia

distractorExplanations.a: Slab-off (bicentric grinding) adds vertical base-up prism at near; it does not address horizontal imbalance.
distractorExplanations.c: Edge thinning in high minus is done with lenticular designs or high index, not with slab-off.
distractorExplanations.d: Image size differences call for iseikonic design (base curve, thickness); slab-off corrects vertical prism at near.

options.b: Back vertex power of the finished lens
options.c: Center thickness of the lens
options.d: Prism and its base direction

distractorExplanations.b: Back vertex power is read on a lensometer; a lens clock measures surface curvature (sag) only.
distractorExplanations.c: Center thickness is measured with thickness calipers; a lens clock reads surface curvature.
distractorExplanations.d: Prism and base direction are found with a lensometer, not with a lens clock.

options.a: Raise the impact resistance of the lens
options.b: Reduce surface reflections
options.c: Improve abrasion resistance
options.d: Block UV transmission

distractorExplanations.a: Hard coats resist surface abrasion; impact resistance depends on lens material and thickness, not the coating.
distractorExplanations.b: Reducing reflections is the job of AR coating, not of the scratch-resistant hard coat.
distractorExplanations.d: UV is blocked by the lens material or a UV absorber; hard coats target surface abrasion.

options.b: The darkness of the tint applied to the lens
options.c: Whether a polarizing film is in the lens
options.d: The color of the AR coating's residual reflex

distractorExplanations.b: A dark tint without a UV absorber can dilate pupils and admit more UV; tint darkness is not UV protection.
distractorExplanations.c: Polarizing film cuts horizontal glare; UV blocking comes from the lens material or a UV absorber.
distractorExplanations.d: The residual AR reflex color is cosmetic and says nothing about how much UV the lens attenuates.

options.a: Adding the cylinder to the sphere and keeping the axis
options.b: Changing the cylinder sign and keeping the axis
options.c: Adding 90° to the axis and keeping the sphere
options.d: Correct sphere/cyl/axis conversion rules

distractorExplanations.a: Transposition adds the cylinder to the sphere and also changes the axis by 90 degrees; the axis cannot stay the same.
distractorExplanations.b: Flipping the cylinder sign alone is incomplete; you must also add cylinder to sphere and change the axis by 90.
distractorExplanations.c: Rotating the axis 90 degrees is one step; the new sphere is sphere plus cylinder, with the cylinder sign reversed.

options.b: Distance between pupils
options.c: Bridge width of the frame
options.d: Distance from pupil to lens back

distractorExplanations.a: Distance between box centers is the frame PD (DBC), a frame measurement, not the patient's pupillary distance.
distractorExplanations.c: Bridge width (DBL) is the distance between the lenses at the bridge, a frame measurement.
distractorExplanations.d: The distance from the eye to the back lens surface is vertex distance, not pupillary distance.

options.a: Position the lens design relative to pupil
options.b: Locate the point where add power is read
options.c: Locate the prism reference point for checking
options.d: Mark where distance power is verified

distractorExplanations.b: Add power is verified in the near circle lower on the lens, not at the fitting cross.
distractorExplanations.c: The prism reference point sits below the fitting cross; prism is checked there, not at the cross.
distractorExplanations.d: Distance power is verified in the distance reference circle above the fitting cross.

options.b: Effective optics and fitting height perception
options.c: The index of refraction of the chosen lens material
options.d: The temple length needed behind the ear

distractorExplanations.a: Pantoscopic tilt is a vertical angle; it does not alter the horizontal PD measurement.
distractorExplanations.c: Index is a fixed material property; tilt changes effective power and induced astigmatism, not index.
distractorExplanations.d: Temple length is a separate frame measurement; tilt alters effective power and fitting height.

options.b: The cylinder axis of the prescription
options.c: The Abbe value of the lens material
options.d: Effective power especially in higher Rx

distractorExplanations.a: Monocular PD is anatomical; moving the lens nearer or farther changes effective power, not the PD.
distractorExplanations.b: Vertex changes effective sphere and cylinder power, not the orientation of the cylinder axis.
distractorExplanations.c: Abbe value is a material constant; vertex distance changes the effective power at the eye.

options.b: Tall frames with a deep B measurement
options.c: Wearers who need wide intermediate zones
options.d: Patients with no near-vision add

distractorExplanations.b: Tall frames with a deep B can fit a standard corridor; short corridors are designed for shallow frames.
distractorExplanations.c: Short corridors compress the intermediate zone, so heavy intermediate users suit longer corridors.
distractorExplanations.d: Without an add there is no corridor at all; a single-vision lens is used instead of a progressive.

options.b: A shift in the cylinder axis
options.c: A change in the sphere power
options.d: A longer vertex distance

distractorExplanations.b: Horizontal decentration does not rotate the cylinder axis; it induces prism per Prentice's rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Decentration leaves the ordered sphere power unchanged; the error is induced prism (Prentice's rule).
distractorExplanations.d: Vertex distance is the lens-to-eye distance set by frame fit, not by a PD mismatch.

options.b: Fit, vertex, and comfort
options.c: Monocular PD of the patient
options.d: Lens power of the Rx

distractorExplanations.a: Temple length is set at the temple bend; nose pads adjust frame height, vertex and comfort.
distractorExplanations.c: Monocular PD is an anatomical measurement; adjusting the pads does not change it.
distractorExplanations.d: Lens power is fixed by the Rx and the finished lens; pads alter fit and position only.

options.a: The power ground into the lenses
options.b: Stability and comfort on the ear
options.c: The bridge width of the frame
options.d: The patient's pupillary distance

distractorExplanations.a: Lens power is set by the surfacing lab; temple bends change fit and stability, not power.
distractorExplanations.c: Bridge width (DBL) is a fixed frame dimension; temples adjust grip and comfort at the ear.
distractorExplanations.d: PD is anatomical; temple adjustments change fit at the ear, not the distance between pupils.

options.a: Standard Rx with no tilt compensation
options.b: Glass lenses for higher impact safety
options.c: Plano lenses with no prescription
options.d: Compensated Rx / fitting considerations

distractorExplanations.a: Face-form wrap induces power and prism changes, so the Rx is often compensated rather than left as written.
distractorExplanations.b: Glass is less impact resistant than polycarbonate or Trivex and is a poor choice for wrap sport frames.
distractorExplanations.c: Many wrap frames can take prescription lenses with compensated designs; they are not limited to plano.

options.b: Single-vision readers with low power
options.c: Progressives and precise optics
options.d: Choosing the frame's bridge size

distractorExplanations.a: Plano sunglasses have no power, so PD placement has no optical effect on them.
distractorExplanations.b: Low-power single-vision readers tolerate small decentration; monocular PDs matter most for progressives.
distractorExplanations.d: Bridge size is chosen by nose fit; monocular PDs set lens centration for each eye.

options.a: Where the optical center sits before the eye
options.b: Where the near segment top sits on the lens
options.c: How far the lens sits from the eye
options.d: How far apart the two optical centers sit

distractorExplanations.b: Segment top placement is seg height, a separate multifocal measurement from OC height.
distractorExplanations.c: Lens-to-eye distance is vertex distance; OC height sets the vertical position of the optical center.
distractorExplanations.d: Horizontal spacing of the optical centers is set by PD; OC height is the vertical position.

options.b: Adult-style progressive lenses by default
options.c: Frames one size larger to allow growth
options.d: CR-39 lenses as the default for impact

distractorExplanations.b: Children rarely need progressives; most get single vision unless a bifocal is prescribed for a specific reason.
distractorExplanations.c: Oversized frames slip and misplace the optical centers; children need a properly sized current fit.
distractorExplanations.d: CR-39 is less impact resistant; polycarbonate or Trivex is preferred for children's lenses.

options.a: Frame color and case match the order
options.b: Power and axis, then file the job
options.c: Fit on face, with power checked next visit
options.d: Power, axis, PD/OC, and fit on face

distractorExplanations.a: Cosmetic items matter, but dispensing verification centers on power, axis, PD/OC and fit.
distractorExplanations.b: Power and axis alone skip PD/OC centration and fit, which also cause wearer complaints.
distractorExplanations.c: Lens power must be verified before release; deferring it means dispensing an unverified Rx.

options.a: Power, axis, and prism of a lens
options.b: Curvature of the corneal surface
options.c: Intraocular pressure of the eye
options.d: Base curve of the front surface

distractorExplanations.b: Corneal curvature is measured with a keratometer, not a lensometer.
distractorExplanations.c: Intraocular pressure is measured with a tonometer; a lensometer reads lens power.
distractorExplanations.d: Front-surface base curve is read with a lens clock; a lensometer reads vertex power, axis and prism.

options.b: Impact standards for safety eyewear
options.c: Contact lens prescription standards
options.d: Nonprescription sunglass and fashion eyewear standards

distractorExplanations.b: Occupational safety eyewear is covered by ANSI Z87.1, not Z80.1.
distractorExplanations.c: Contact lenses fall under ANSI Z80.20; Z80.1 covers prescription spectacle lenses.
distractorExplanations.d: Nonprescription sunglasses fall under ANSI Z80.3; Z80.1 covers prescription spectacle lenses.

options.b: A tool for measuring vertex distance
options.c: A tool for reading lens power
options.d: A gauge for lens center thickness

distractorExplanations.b: Vertex distance is measured with a distometer; a PD ruler measures pupil distance.
distractorExplanations.c: Lens power is read on a lensometer; the PD ruler measures distances on the face.
distractorExplanations.d: Center thickness is measured with calipers; a PD ruler cannot measure lens thickness.

options.a: Surfaces the Rx curves onto the lens back
options.b: Applies the AR and hard coatings
options.c: Measures the patient's PD and heights
options.d: Captures shape and cuts lens to fit

distractorExplanations.a: Rx curves are generated in surfacing; the tracer/edger works on finished lens blanks.
distractorExplanations.b: Coatings are applied in coating chambers; tracing and edging handle frame shape and cutting.
distractorExplanations.c: PD and heights come from patient measurement; the tracer captures frame shape.

options.a: Finished lens matches the ordered Rx
options.b: Frame fits the patient's face and ears
options.c: The patient's subjective refraction
options.d: Lens material matches the stated index

distractorExplanations.b: Facial fit is checked in the dispensing adjustment, not by lensometer neutralization.
distractorExplanations.c: Subjective refraction is done by the eye doctor; neutralization checks the finished lens against the order.
distractorExplanations.d: Material index is not read by neutralization, which measures power, axis and prism against the Rx.

options.a: Lensometer dots at the optical center
options.b: Layout/marking tools per manufacturer charts
options.c: A ruler from the lens geometric center
options.d: Marks copied from the patient's old pair

distractorExplanations.a: Lensometer dots mark the optical center; on a progressive the fitting cross is relocated from engravings and the chart.
distractorExplanations.c: The geometric center is not the fitting cross; progressive layout uses the hidden engravings and the chart.
distractorExplanations.d: Old-pair marks may reflect a different design or fit; recreate the crosses from the manufacturer chart.

options.b: Adjust zyl frames safely
options.c: Cure the hard coat on new lenses
options.d: Soften polycarbonate lenses for edging

distractorExplanations.a: Titanium is adjusted cold with pliers; heat is for cellulose acetate (zyl) frames.
distractorExplanations.c: Hard coats are cured in the lab; frame warmers soften plastic frames for adjustment.
distractorExplanations.d: Polycarbonate lenses are edged dry without heat; heating them can damage the coatings.

options.a: Dispense if the patient reads 20/20 at pickup
options.b: Dispense and note the variance in the chart
options.c: Re-mark the lens and recheck it next visit
options.d: Do not dispense until resolved

distractorExplanations.a: Acuity at pickup does not prove the lens matches the Rx; out-of-tolerance lenses go back for remake.
distractorExplanations.b: Documenting a variance does not make an out-of-tolerance lens acceptable to dispense.
distractorExplanations.c: Deferring the recheck means dispensing a lens that has not passed verification.

options.a: Rx tolerance limits for dress lenses
options.b: Corridor length for progressive lenses
options.c: Impact and coverage requirements
options.d: AR coating durability requirements

distractorExplanations.a: Dress-lens Rx tolerances come from ANSI Z80.1; safety standards like Z87.1 cover impact and coverage.
distractorExplanations.b: Corridor length is a lens design choice; safety standards govern impact resistance and coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: AR durability is a quality specification; safety standards address impact resistance and coverage.

options.a: Share Rx details with family who ask
options.b: Email full Rx records to any requester
options.c: Protect records but discuss cases openly
options.d: Protect PHI in records and conversations

distractorExplanations.a: Family members need patient authorization (or a recognized role) before receiving protected health information.
distractorExplanations.b: PHI may be released to authorized requesters; sending records to anyone who asks violates HIPAA.
distractorExplanations.c: Spoken information is PHI too; HIPAA protection covers conversations as well as written records.

options.a: Clean tools once at the end of each day
options.b: Clean frames only when visibly soiled
options.c: Wipe pads with water before the next fitting
options.d: Clean frames/tools between patients

distractorExplanations.a: End-of-day cleaning leaves tools contaminated from one patient to the next during the day.
distractorExplanations.b: Contamination is often invisible, so every frame and tool is cleaned between patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Plain water does not disinfect; use an approved disinfectant between patients.

abo-optician-readiness-check-instruments.explanation: Clean frames/tools between patients as policy requires; visible cleanliness or end-of-day cleaning is not enough.

options.b: The patient's complaint and new order date
options.c: Lab invoice number and remake charges
options.d: The staff member's name and lab used

distractorExplanations.b: Complaint and date alone miss the measurements and verification needed to find the cause of the remake.
distractorExplanations.c: Billing details track cost but do not show what was measured or why the job failed.
distractorExplanations.d: Staff and lab names omit the measurements and reason codes needed for remake analysis.
